title: Anyone use Tripo? I am struggling to get a useful model or texture.
author: PoopsMcScoots
selftext:
So I paid for a month of Tripo because I was interested in their smart texture option.

Well, it’s not. Smart that is.

Of course it’s all marketing lies.

And of course all their example models are flagrant lies that there’s no way we’re prompted.

The model is just a jumble of nonsense.

Nonsymetrical, holes everywhere, unnecessary triangles everywhere, no sharp edges, and just about every problem you can imagine.

I just spent 8 hours fixing a model and realized that I could have just made it in this time.

I think the I just need to give up on the smart mesh option and redo typology myself in Blender.

I’m not much on an artist by I can at least do that.

But that still leave UV unwrapping and texturing.

And it’s also lousy at that.

There’s no option to explicitly tell it where you want certain seams. So back to blender because it’s bad at that too!

Then I drag it back in and I’m not seeing an option for it to repack my UV. SO BACK TO BLENDER YET AGAIN!

Finally I send it back and to do the textures.

And guess what?

Complete shit!

Time to open Gimp and fix it.

And then yeah, back to Blender.

So at this point, WHAT THE FUCK AM I EVEN PAYING THEM FOR???

Am I just missing something?

Oh, and nana banana had me screaming at the monitor. Apparently “make their backpack slightly larger” means make it larger than the player.

replies.author: Furyan9x
replies.body:
I think this is an ironic comment, because I was just about to comment that Tripo has been the best for me, out of the 3 I tried: meshy first, did not give me what I wanted with a bunch of tries (10+, using Claude and Gemini to write my prompts and provide reference images), so Gemini told me to try 3d AI Studio, so I subbed to that. It was slightly better than meshy (even using their own meshy wrapper), but still not good. Then CLAUDE told me to just use tripo directly, because the wrapper could be causing issues. So finally I subbed to tripo and with a bit of work on my part using the various tools, I got pretty good models for humans, armor, a couple weapons, a couple static objects, a couple capes. 

I think AI is just too unpredictable and there's too many variables to compare them accurately.

comments.author: CycleMother2006
comments.body:
Tripo is incredible and has absurdly good topology... But only for easily definable objects. Complex pieces need to be separated out. For instance, if you're genning a character you have to do the head separately from the body. Clothing needs its own gens, etc.

And no generator out there will do a good job with something like architecture. Should be creating separated building kits for that.

So yes you're probably missing something. Either trying to generate something too complex for the allotted polys, or possibly your images themselves are not providing a clear enough foundation to work with. There are a lot of things that can go wrong on this front.

I saw you mentioned something about armor suits in a post in the thread. Try using smart mesh to JUST generate a helmet. Then JUST a gauntlet, then a boot, pants, and cuirass.  Those are all meant to be separate modular pieces. You might be able to get it to make a armored knight as a full creature-kind-of-thing, but it won't be a proper suit of armor to put on a character unless you split it.

These tools have horrible parts-splitting capabilities. The only one that comes kind of close to being workable on that front is Rodin, and then you're still dealing with poor topology and a lot of manual corrections.

Where these tools best shine, imo, is for static props, or equipment like swords/shields, etc. And you can make anything work as long as you chunk it into a small enough--yet understandable--breakdown of chunks. But each chunk has to be identifiable for what it is.

So don't  prompt an ornate bookshelf with books. Prompt the ornate shelf, then prompt the things that go on the shelf one by one (or, more likely, just make most of those in blender because it's best with low-detail, primitive shaped things like books, candles, etc.)

replies.author: PoopsMcScoots
replies.body:
Thank you for the tips. I’ll give them a try.

I will save one of the issues I keep seeing that makes bizarre choices for topology when you have something on top of something else.

Like a utility belt for example.

replies.author: CycleMother2006
replies.body: That's a good observation with the utility belt. And yes, it's VERY bad with layering things. This is especially where texture falls apart. I'm pretty sure these models use projection methods to texture meshes, which means they fall apart at creases or overlaps. Geometry tends to fuse together in those places as well, leaning towards creating one seamless mesh instead of separate parts. This also leads to awkward topology in those areas where it's trying to continue edge loops from, say, a waist, into a belt, and that can make animation wonky.  This really isn't a problem if people are reusing the assets as modular pieces anyway (this is my case, and why it doesn't bother me) but I can see where it could get frustrating if you're making a game that doesn't need that and would prefer to just one-shot interesting character designs in one-go and let each batch be simpler as a self-contained entity.

comments.author: fhtiek
comments.body:
Meshy is the only one worth a damn right now unfortunately. Their most recent model is actually quite good. However. i find you really jave to generate the high-poly flagship and then remesh it down to the topology you need. The "game ready" model is a lot more volatile on details i find and needs a lot more work after the fact vs doing the high fidelity then using the remesh tool.

The rigging isnt bad either, but using claude + blender MCP is definitely an inprovement for making rigs. That being said, even with mcp you will have to iterate a lot unless its a humanoid. The more uncommon the silhouette the more trouble it will jave

comments.author: UncleJoesLandscaping
comments.body:
I guess it depends on your use case. With chatgpt images as input, Tripo has given me 10/10 for items and 7/10 for furniture. I was even impresses with the characters they made, even though they needed some post proc
essing.

comments.author: strawberry-ramune
comments.body: I think most people are approaching this issue the wrong way. If you're going to build a lego car, you don't generate the car and then try to separate it into bricks. You'd start with defining a brick and what rules they're going to have, and then create a system for constructing things out of them. I think at the moment the 2D-3D modeling engines are kind of a dead end if you need anything reusable. It's just going to be a money pit that locks you into using their service forever.
